beats.say: What happens to your index funds when WTI crude oil drops 1.90% to $91.11 before you lose money?
Most investors panic when energy prices slide, missing the hidden margin relief flowing straight into retail index holdings.
When WTI crude falls 1.41% over five days down to $91.11, transportation costs shrink for every major consumer basket.
That means lower operating overhead for your S&P 500 index funds, protecting your portfolio from sudden shocks.
This is not financial advice, but when you review your assets, remember lower oil costs drive margin relief. Subscribe to Why Stocks Moved.

teardown.hook: How does Costco make almost zero profit on gasoline, but its stock still surged to a four hundred billion dollar valuation before you buy shares?
teardown.hook_why: It uses a familiar consumer product (cheap gas) to present a non-obvious corporate mechanism (membership model driving a $400B valuation gap), instantly triggering curiosity and FOMO.

beats.said: How does Costco make almost zero profit on gasoline, but its stock still surged to a four hundred billion dollar valuation before you buy shares?
beats.shown: Moving stock chart of COST rising, with a giant overlay of a gas pump icon and '$0.00 Profit' text.

beats.said: Most stations live and die by gas margins. But Costco uses cheap fuel as a loss leader to get you past the pump and inside the warehouse.
beats.shown: A split screen showing a gas pump cutting rapidly to a Costco warehouse floor chart showing foot traffic correlation.

beats.said: Once you are inside, the real magic happens. Ninety percent of Costco’s actual operating income doesn't come from selling goods—it comes from membership fees.
beats.shown: A clean bar chart breaking down Costco's revenue vs. net profit from membership fees, highlighting 90% in bright yellow.

beats.said: That recurring fee revenue is highly predictable, which is why Wall Street values this stock at a premium compared to traditional retail giants.
beats.shown: Chart comparing COST valuation multiples against Walmart and Target, highlighting Costco's massive premium.

beats.said: This is not financial advice, but when you look at retail stocks, look at what drives the foot traffic, not just the sticker price.
beats.shown: Zooming out of the COST stock chart to show the final CTA: 'Subscribe to Why Stocks Moved'.

teardown.pacing: High-velocity cuts every 3-4 seconds. Pacing is fast and structured to hold attention, slowing down slightly at the 18s mark to explain the valuation multiple before the quick wrap-up.
teardown.visual_technique: Split-screen comparison, clean line charts, bright highlighter overlays on SEC filing data, and a moving stock chart from frame zero.
reusable_moves: The Everyday Contrast: Open with an incredibly cheap consumer item to explain a massive, high-valuation stock movement.
The Margin Trap: Pivot from low product margins to high-margin recurring revenue models that Wall Street actually prices in.
The Chart First Rule: Start with a moving ticker chart at frame zero to signal immediate financial relevance.
teardown.remake_plan: Remake the $5B Twinkies problem into a Costco gas-to-membership stock teardown, using a moving COST chart at frame zero to explain why low-margin fuel drives a $400B market cap.
